newsitem.title: USA: Perot blasts Clinton, Dole on special interests.
newsitem.headline: Perot blasts Clinton, Dole on special interests.

text.p: Ross Perot, hoping to nudge his struggling candidacy into the limelight of the presidential debate, charged the two major party candidates Wednesday with ignoring "the real problem" of the influence of special interests on the 1996 campaign.

During a town-hall style meeting with voters aired on CNN's "Larry King Live" talk show, the Texas billioinaire echoed calls by a public advocacy group for a probe of questionable campaign contributions to both the Republican and Democratic parties.

"They didn't even bring it up tonight. Isn't that interesting?" Perot told a studio audience in an appearance that followed on the heels of the second 90-minute debate between President Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole.

"Both parties are bought and paid for by the special interests. We've got to get the special interest money out of politics. We've got to have the only people who count be the voters and the people back home in the districts."

Perot, who is running for president as the self-financed candidate of the nascent Reform Party, referred to a new report by the Washington-based watchdog group Common Cause that questions the legality of campaign contributions accepted by the two major parties in the 1996 campaign.
"We have people trapped in a bad system that is designed to produce the result where only 19 percent of the American people trust their government," he said.

The long-simmering issue of campaign financing erupted anew this month with news accounts of hefty contributions to the Democratic Party from a wealthy Indonesian family with personal ties to Clinton.

Perot, who took part in three presidential debates in 1992 and went on to capture 19 percent of the vote, fielded questions from the CNN audience for about 45 minutes in a bid to boost his support in national opinion polls from the low single digits.

The King programme later included three other minority party candidates -- Harry Browne of the Libertarian Party, John Hagelin of the Natural Law Party and Howard Phillips of the U.S. Taxpayers Party.
Those candidates were all excluded from the formal debate process this year, along with Perot and Green Party candidate Ralph Nader.
Perot also criticised Clinton, Dole and their rhetoric about balanced budgets for avoiding the issue of the overall national debt, which currently stands at $5 trillion.
"They talk about all these balancing the budgets and what have you. But they say from their own government numbers that the debt will have gone up to $8 trillion by the year 2005."
